title: Frame a gain against normal growth
statement: Judge any gain against the growth that students with the same starting score, grade and weeks of instruction make anyway, which is small for stronger students in later grades.
example: At or above the 50th percentile in grades 6 and up, expected growth on one widely used test flattens toward 1–2 points.
detail: Two course designs in one program, for Grade 7 reading and Grade 7–8 prealgebra, carry the same caveat relayed from a recap: at the 50th percentile and above in grades 6 and up, expected growth on the outside test flattens toward 1–2 points. The reading design says its projections must be framed against that lower base rate or they will look inflated, under its rule to predict direction, not magnitude, before an in-cohort pilot; the prealgebra design says to frame pilot expectations accordingly.
against: Neither design gives the period the 1–2 points cover, and both relay the figure from a recap rather than measure it. The package itself withholds conditional growth percentiles until its own scale has been linked to the reference test's (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/map-proxy-assessment/validity/00_BRAINLIFT.md`, line 37), so until then this judgement rests on the official test.

evidence.quote: at the 50th percentile and above in grades 6+, expected MAP growth flattens toward 1–2 points — G7 projections must be framed against that lower base rate, or they'll look inflated.
at ≥50th percentile in 6+, expected MAP growth flattens to 1–2 points — frame pilot expectations accordingly.
MAP's key diagnostic output is the Conditional Growth Percentile (CGP): how much a student grew relative to academically matched peers (same prior RIT, same grade, same weeks of instruction).
it controls for starting ability and asks whether the student grew more or less than expected

citations.ref: NWEA (2025), MAP Growth Norms Technical Manual
